items.question: When do you use Task.Run versus async/await?
items.answer: async/await frees threads during I/O — network, disk, database. Task.Run queues CPU-bound work to the thread pool so you do not block the ASP.NET request thread during hashing or parsing. Do not Task.Run an already async method just to be async. Parallel and PLINQ partition CPU work across cores when each item is expensive enough to justify coordination overhead.
followUps: What happens if you Parallel.ForEach inside a request that already uses the thread pool heavily?

items.sixtySeconds: async for I/O wait. Task.Run for CPU on pool. Never confuse them. PLINQ for big CPU-bound LINQ.

items.question: Why must you never lock across an await?
items.answer: lock is thread-scoped mutual exclusion. await releases the thread but does not release lock — other threads block on the lock while the holder is not even running. Under load you serialize the entire service and can deadlock with the thread pool. Release the lock before any I/O. Use SemaphoreSlim for throttling concurrent outbound calls instead of holding Monitor across network waits.
followUps: Can you use lock with Monitor.TryEnter and timeout?
What is the difference between lock and SemaphoreSlim?
items.sixtySeconds: lock plus await equals disaster. Short lock for memory only. Throttle I/O with SemaphoreSlim.

items.question: When is volatile enough, and when do you need Interlocked or lock?
items.answer: volatile ensures reads and writes of one field are not cached in a CPU register indefinitely — good for shutdown flags. It does not make compound operations like check-then-act atomic. Interlocked provides atomic read-modify-write for counters and CompareExchange for lazy initialization. lock protects multi-field invariants. Monitor exit publishes writes with a full memory barrier.
followUps: Does lock make volatile redundant inside the critical section?
items.sixtySeconds: volatile for single flag visibility. Interlocked for counters. lock for invariants. Never volatile for increment.

items.question: ReaderWriterLockSlim versus ConcurrentDictionary — when do you pick each?
items.answer: ReaderWriterLockSlim fits read-heavy data with rare bulk reload — many readers share the read lock, one writer takes exclusive lock. ConcurrentDictionary fits per-key churn and cache maps with continuous updates. Wrong choice: RW lock on a hot mutable map where writers block all readers constantly. Profile lock contention with dotnet-counters before micro-optimizing.
followUps: Can you await while holding a read lock?
What is lock striping in ConcurrentDictionary?
items.sixtySeconds: RW lock for rare reload, many readers. ConcurrentDictionary for per-key updates. Not RW lock on hot writes.

items.question: How do you fix a Redis cache stampede when traffic spikes?
items.answer: Many parallel cache misses on the same key each hit the database. Single-flight: ConcurrentDictionary of in-flight Task per key so one loader runs and others await the same Task. Add SemaphoreSlim to cap total database concurrency across keys. Jitter cache TTL. Never wrap Redis get and database query in one global lock — that serializes all keys.
followUps: How is single-flight like Promise deduplication in TypeScript?

items.sixtySeconds: Per-key Task coalescing. DB semaphore. No global lock on cache path.

items.question: When would you choose Channel over ConcurrentQueue plus lock?
items.answer: Channel gives async WriteAsync and ReadAllAsync with optional bounded capacity for backpressure. A RabbitMQ receiver can write to a channel and multiple workers read without hand-rolled wait handles. ConcurrentQueue is lower level; you still coordinate completion and blocking. Channels fit producer-consumer pipelines; ConcurrentDictionary fits shared maps.
followUps: How does Channel relate to IAsyncEnumerable?
items.sixtySeconds: Channel for async producer-consumer with backpressure. ConcurrentDictionary for shared maps.

items.question: Your service deadlocks under load after adding sync-over-async — diagnose it.
items.answer: Capture dotnet-dump thread stacks. Look for threads blocked on Monitor.Wait while another thread waits on Task.Wait or .Result — classic pool deadlock. Fix: async all the way, ConfigureAwait(false) in libraries, never .Result inside lock. Fixed global lock order when multiple locks are unavoidable.
followUps: Does ASP.NET Core have a SynchronizationContext?
How does lock ordering prevent circular wait?
items.sixtySeconds: Dump threads. Monitor plus Result equals deadlock. Async end-to-end. Fixed lock order.

items.question: How do you prove thread pool starvation in production?
items.answer: dotnet-counters on System.Runtime: threadpool-queue-length and threadpool-thread-count rising while CPU is flat suggests blocking on pool threads — sync I/O, .Result, or lock convoys. Latency rises on unrelated endpoints because continuations queue behind blocked workers. Fix root cause: true async I/O, remove blocking waits, shorten critical sections.
followUps: What is hill-climbing in the thread pool?

items.sixtySeconds: Queue length up, CPU flat — blocking on pool. dotnet-counters. Fix async and locks.
